blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
An experiment is any process whose result is not known in advance: rolling a die, testing a child for anaemia, recording next month’s case count. Each possible result is an outcome. The set of all outcomes is the sample space, written S. An event is any collection of outcomes, that is, any subset of S. Probability is a number P(A) attached to every event A that obeys three axioms (rules accepted without proof, from which everything else is derived):

  1. Non-negativity: P(A) ≥ 0 for every event A.
  2. Total probability one: P(S) = 1. Something in the sample space must happen.
  3. Additivity: if A and B cannot happen together (they share no outcomes), then P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The sample space is the list of everything that could happen. An event is a question you can ask of the result (“is the die even?”), answered yes by some outcomes and no by others. The axioms say only three things: probabilities are never negative, the whole sample space has probability 1, and probabilities of non-overlapping events add. Every rule in this chapter (the complement rule, the addition rule, Bayes’ theorem) is a consequence of these three lines. The axioms do not say where the numbers come from. Three approaches supply them: counting equally likely outcomes (§5.1.1), observing long-run frequencies (§5.1.2) and personal judgement (§5.1.3). All three obey the same axioms, so the same rules apply to all of them.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Rolling one die: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. The event “even” is A = {2, 4, 6}; the event “4” is {4}. Testing one child for anaemia: S = {anaemic, not anaemic}. Counting malaria cases in a village next month: S = {0, 1, 2, 3, …}, a sample space with no upper limit.

points.html: Two consequences follow at once from the axioms. Every probability lies between 0 and 1 (the upper bound is derived in §5.2.3). The probability of an impossible event is 0.
Write the sample space down before calculating. Many errors in probability problems come from a sample space that is vague or that silently omits outcomes.

Events are sets, so the words “or”, “and” and “not” have set meanings: “A or B” means at least one of them happens; “A and B” means both happen; “not A” (the complement) means every outcome outside A.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Classical (a priori) probability assumes all outcomes in a finite sample space are equally likely, and defines P(A) = (number of outcomes in A) ÷ (total number of outcomes).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: This is probability by reasoning about the structure of a situation, before any data exist. A fair coin has two symmetric sides, so heads has probability 1/2 before anyone flips it. The formula satisfies the three axioms automatically: counts are never negative, the whole sample space counts n/n = 1, and counts of non-overlapping sets add.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A fair die has 6 equally likely outcomes. P(even) = 3/6 = 0.5. P(at least 5) = 2/6 = 0.333. No die was rolled.

blocks.alt: Classical probability: outcomes of a fair die
blocks.caption: Figure 5.1. Classical probability: the six equally likely outcomes of a fair die.

points.html: Formula: P(A) = (favourable outcomes) ÷ (total equally likely outcomes).

The equal-likelihood assumption is the whole method. It fails for a loaded die, and it has no meaning for “will this patient develop a rash?”, where the outcomes are not symmetric. Then empirical probability (§5.1.2) is needed.
Counting outcomes quickly becomes hard when there are many; the counting rules in §5.7.1.2 handle that.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Empirical (relative frequency) probability estimates P(A) by the proportion of times A occurred in a large number of repetitions: P(A) ≈ (number of times A occurred) ÷ (number of trials).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: You cannot reason your way to the probability that a patient develops a drug rash, as you can for a fair coin. So you observe: out of many patients given the drug, what fraction developed the rash? The observed fraction is your estimate of the true probability. It is an estimate, not the probability itself. A second group of 500 patients would give a slightly different fraction, just as a second sample gives a different statistic for the same parameter (recall §1.3).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Of 500 patients who received an antibiotic, 15 developed a rash. Empirical P(rash) = 15/500 = 0.03. At an anganwadi, 36 of 400 children screened have pallor: empirical P(pallor) = 36/400 = 0.09.

points.html: The estimate settles down as trials accumulate. The precise statement is the (weak) law of large numbers: as the number of independent repetitions grows, the probability that the observed proportion differs from the true probability by more than any small amount you choose shrinks towards zero. The law says nothing about the next single trial. After ten boys, the next birth is not “due” to be a girl.
Prevalence, treatment-response rates, sensitivity and specificity are all empirical probabilities, estimated from data.
How far an estimate from one sample is likely to be from the truth is the subject of sampling distributions and standard errors (the spread of a statistic over repeated samples, §6.5–§6.7).

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Subjective probability is a person’s degree of belief that an event will occur, based on judgement and the information available, rather than on counting or repeated observation.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Some events are one-off and cannot be repeated or reasoned out from symmetry. An experienced clinician who says “this patient has about a 70% chance of responding” is stating a subjective probability. It is still a probability: if it is coherent, it obeys the same three axioms, so it can be combined with the rules that follow.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Before any case data arrive, a district epidemiologist judges that a new outbreak has “about a 20% chance” of becoming a large epidemic. The number guides immediate planning; it will be revised as cases are counted (the revision rule is Bayes’ theorem, §5.5).

points.html: Two equally informed, reasonable people can hold different subjective probabilities. That is the key difference from classical and empirical probability.
Subjective probability is the starting point of Bayesian statistics (inference that updates a prior belief with data, §15.8). A clinician’s pre-test probability in §5.5 is often subjective.

questions.prompt: A clinician says “I think this patient has about a 70% chance of responding to treatment”, based on years of experience with similar cases. Which approach to probability is this, and why can it not be classical probability?
questions.answer: Subjective probability: a degree of belief built from judgement and experience. It cannot be classical, because classical probability needs a finite set of equally likely outcomes that can be counted, and a single patient’s response has no such symmetric structure. (Nor is it strictly empirical: no count of repeated trials was made, although the clinician’s experience is informal evidence of that kind.)

questions.prompt: Write down the sample space for “number of ANC visits a woman makes, capped at 4 or more”. Which of the three axioms tells you the probabilities of its outcomes must add to 1?
questions.answer: S = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or more}. The outcomes do not overlap and together make up S, so by additivity (axiom 3) their probabilities add to P(S), which is 1 by axiom 2 (total probability one).

questions.prompt: In a village survey, 54 of 600 adults report a diagnosis of hypertension. What is the empirical probability of a reported diagnosis? Would a second survey of 600 adults give exactly the same number? Which law describes what happens to the estimate as the survey grows?
questions.answer: 54 ÷ 600 = 0.09. A second survey of 600 would almost certainly give a slightly different proportion, because each sample gives its own statistic for the same parameter. The (weak) law of large numbers says that as the number of people surveyed grows, the chance that the observed proportion is far from the true probability shrinks towards zero.
